Overview

Portal hypertension is increased pressure within the portal venous system

Pressure difference of 6 mmHg or more between the portal vein and the inferior vena cava confirms portal hypertension diagnosis

Liver cirrhosis is the most common cause for portal hypertension

Pathophysiology

Portal vein collects blood from bowel and go through the liver and into the hepatic vein and then to inferior vena cava

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Portal hypertension develops when the resistance to the portal blood flow increases leading to increase the pressure difference between portal and inferior vena cava

Resistance could be in the liver in form of cirrhosis, or it could be prehepatic in the portal vein in form of portal vein thrombosis, or it could be post hepatic like Budd Chiari syndrome (occlusion of the hepatic vein)

When the portal blood pressure remains elevated, body tries to decrease this pressure by opening the collateral vessels that bypass the liver’s normal circulation (thus bypassing the resistance), examples of the collaterals include:

  • Esophageal varices
  • Gastric varices
  • Rectal varices
  • Periumbilical veins (caput medusa)
  • Splenic collaterals
  • Retroperitoneal collaterals

Causes

Prehepatic: portal vein thrombosis, arteriovenous malformations or fistulas involving the portal vein

Intrahepatic: congenital hepatic fibrosis, schistosomiasis, liver cirrhosis, veno-occlusive disease

Post hepatic: Budd-Chiari syndrome, inferior vena cava obstruction, constrictive pericarditis

Clinical features

No symptoms until complications arise

Cirrhosis is the most common cause of portal hypertension and when patient have it, they present with jaundice, palmar erythema, spider nevi, gynecomastia, ascites, asterixis and hepatic encephalopathy

Patient might present with hematemesis or melena from bleeding varices

Splenomegaly is reliable sign in the diagnosis of portal hypertension, if no splenomegaly think of other differential diagnosis

Diagnosis

CBC to look for anemia from bleeding, thrombocytopenia from bleeding or liver failure

LFT, RFT looking for liver or renal failure

Coagulation profile to look for deficiencies in the coagulation factors from liver failure

Doppler US of the portal vein looking for stenosis or thrombosis

Abdominal US looking for liver cirrhosis, ascites and splenomegaly

Endoscopy looking for varices

Patient with ascites need paracentesis to look for the cause

Measurement of portal pressure often not required to make the diagnosis because the clinical features are enough

Treatment

Treat the cause: e.g. portal vein thrombosis treated with anticoagulation, liver cirrhosis treated with liver transplantation

Treat the complications: e.g. hematemesis treated with supportive measures (blood transfusions…) and endoscopic therapy

Empiric antibiotics for prophylaxis against SBP

Ascites treated with sodium restriction, diuretics and paracentesis
